title: Bliki: Generated Glossary
author: Martin Fowler
summary: When we use LLMs in a specialized domain, such as the operations of any reasonably-large organization, there is a lot of specialized vocabulary. Such words and specialized meanings will be foreign to an LLM because they aren't in its training set, making it harder for the LLM to be effective when doing tasks in that domain. One technique to aid this is to use an LLM to generate a glossary of the terminology in that domain, and make this glossary available for any LLMs doing work in those circumstances. The sources for the LLM can be any material within the organization concerned such as documents, emails, and chat logs. In some cases getting transcripts of audio or video may be helpful, although most organizations generate enough text to do the job. The glossary-generating LLM should look for single words, and phrases of several words that regularly hang out together to form a meaningful term. The generator should be asked to identify terms that are new to it, but also known terms that are being used in unfamiliar ways. The latter can often cause the most confusion. title: BigQuery measures is now GA: Unifying BI metrics and knowledge graphs for AI accuracy
summary: To answer a complex business question, an AI agent must understand two things: what happened, and why. The what is a governed metric, like revenue at risk; the why is the network of relationships that produced it. Because metric definitions, a.k.a. measures, traditionally live in business intelligence (BI) platforms while relationships live in knowledge graphs, an AI agent only ever sees half the picture. It guesses the rest, leading to confident but sometimes wrong answers. To solve this hallucination problem, we introduced measures in BigQuery, which are now generally available. Historically, organizations needing both BI and knowledge graphs had to run two siloed technology stacks: one to calculate reliable metrics, the other to map out entity relationships. Bridging them entailed brittle data pipelines and runtime reconciliation by analysts and AI agents, who held the connections in their heads or in sprawling prompts. This patchwork approach wasn't just slow and expensive — it’s where data governance broke down, as every analyst and prompt may define joins and metrics differently. summary: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away. I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior... And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely!
